```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(randomForest)
library(pROC)

options(width = 110)

usc_red  <- "#990000"
usc_gold <- "#E69F00"
blue     <- "#0072B2"

# --- the churn data: 3,000 customers of a subscription business ---
churn <- fread("data/churn_data.csv")
churn[, region := factor(region)]
churn_rate <- mean(churn$churn)

plain_names <- c(
  tenure_months      = "tenure (months)",
  logins_last30      = "logins, last 30 days",
  tickets_30d        = "support tickets, last 30 days",
  email_engagement   = "email engagement (0 to 1)",
  price_increase_60d = "price increase, last 60 days",
  plan_downgrade     = "plan downgrade",
  region             = "region")

# --- stratified 70/30 train/test split ---
set.seed(123)
idx_pos <- which(churn$churn == 1)
idx_neg <- which(churn$churn == 0)
train_id <- sort(c(sample(idx_pos, floor(0.7 * length(idx_pos))),
                   sample(idx_neg, floor(0.7 * length(idx_neg)))))
train <- churn[train_id]
test  <- churn[-train_id]

# --- two models: logit and random forest ---
logit_fit <- glm(churn ~ ., data = train, family = binomial())
set.seed(123)
rf_fit <- randomForest(factor(churn) ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300, importance = TRUE)

test[, p_logit := predict(logit_fit, newdata = test, type = "response")]
test[, p_rf    := predict(rf_fit, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "1"]]

# --- metric helpers ---
conf_metrics <- function(y, p, thr = 0.5) {
  yhat <- as.integer(p >= thr)
  TP <- sum(yhat == 1 & y == 1); FP <- sum(yhat == 1 & y == 0)
  FN <- sum(yhat == 0 & y == 1); TN <- sum(yhat == 0 & y == 0)
  acc  <- (TP + TN) / length(y)
  prec <- ifelse(TP + FP == 0, NA, TP / (TP + FP))
  rec  <- ifelse(TP + FN == 0, NA, TP / (TP + FN))
  f1   <- ifelse(is.na(prec) | is.na(rec) | prec + rec == 0, NA,
                 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec))
  data.table(TP = TP, FP = FP, FN = FN, TN = TN,
             accuracy = acc, precision = prec, recall = rec, f1 = f1)
}
m_logit <- conf_metrics(test$churn, test$p_logit)
m_rf    <- conf_metrics(test$churn, test$p_rf)

roc_logit <- roc(test$churn, test$p_logit, quiet = TRUE)
roc_rf    <- roc(test$churn, test$p_rf,    quiet = TRUE)
auc_logit <- as.numeric(auc(roc_logit))
auc_rf    <- as.numeric(auc(roc_rf))

# --- the threshold sweep for the precision-recall tradeoff ---
sweep <- rbindlist(lapply(seq(0.05, 0.60, by = 0.01), function(t)
  cbind(thr = t, conf_metrics(test$churn, test$p_logit, t))))
sweep <- sweep[!is.na(precision)]

# --- the worked threshold pick: lowest threshold with precision >= 50% ---
pick <- sweep[precision >= 0.5][thr == min(thr)]

# --- odds ratios (logit), with plain labels ---
or <- data.table(term = names(coef(logit_fit)), beta = coef(logit_fit))[term != "(Intercept)"]
or_labels <- c(
  tenure_months      = "tenure (per extra month)",
  logins_last30      = "logins last 30 days (per extra login)",
  tickets_30d        = "support tickets (per extra ticket)",
  email_engagement   = "email engagement (0 to 1)",
  price_increase_60d = "price increase in last 60 days (yes vs. no)",
  plan_downgrade     = "plan downgrade (yes vs. no)",
  regionNorth        = "region: North (vs. East)",
  regionSouth        = "region: South (vs. East)",
  regionWest         = "region: West (vs. East)")
or[, label := or_labels[term]]
or[, odds := exp(beta)]
or <- or[!grepl("^region", term)]        # keep the deck readable: drop region dummies
or <- or[order(odds)]
or[, label := factor(label, levels = label)]

# --- random forest importance, with plain labels ---
imp <- data.table(term = rownames(importance(rf_fit)),
                  gain = importance(rf_fit)[, "MeanDecreaseAccuracy"])
imp[, label := plain_names[term]]
imp <- imp[order(gain)]
imp[, label := factor(label, levels = label)]

# --- the ad-click exercise data, for the practice slide ---
ad <- fread("data/ad_click_data.csv")

# --- capacity view: the retention team can contact the top 10% ---
K <- ceiling(0.10 * nrow(test))
top_rf <- test[order(-p_rf)][1:K]
prec_k <- mean(top_rf$churn)
rec_k  <- sum(top_rf$churn) / sum(test$churn)

fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 0)
  ifelse(is.na(x), "undefined", sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x))
```

# Before We Start {.divider}

## Housekeeping

- **Project proposals**: feedback and grades are posted on Brightspace
  (Assignments → Project: Proposal presentation)
- **Homework 3** due **Thursday, Oct. 29**
- **Thursday**: guest speaker **Hong Zhang**, Marketing Data Science Manager
  at **Netflix**. Come with questions
- Today: **classifiers**, models that predict who will do what

## From explaining to predicting {.smaller-90}

So far every model answered "**what drives** Y": what drives price, what
drives the chance a listing is a gem. We read **coefficients** and told a
story about the market.

Today we ask a different question: "**who will do it?**"

- Which customers will **cancel** next month? (churn: yes/no)
- Who will **click** this ad? Who will **use** the coupon?
- Which reviews are **fake** and which are organic?

::: {.box}
Same tools, different goal: we no longer care only about *why*. We care
whether the model can **call the right names**, customer by customer,
so marketing can act: who gets the retention offer, the ad, the audit.
:::

## What is a classifier? {.smaller-90}

A **classifier** is a model that assigns each customer (each row) to a
**class**, a bucket:

| Kind | Classes | Marketing example |
|---|---|------|
| **Binary** | 2 | churn vs. stay, click vs. no click |
| **Multi-class** | 3 or more | which ad (A, B, or C), which product category |
| **Ordinal** | ordered | star rating (1 to 5) |

- Inputs are **features**: tenure, logins, past purchases, ad impressions
- Output is a **predicted class**, usually through a **probability**:
  the model says $p(\text{churn}) = 0.72$, and a **decision rule** turns it
  into a label: if $p \geq 0.5$, predict "churn"

::: {.box}
You already built one. The **logit** from week 5 outputs a probability:
add a cutoff, and it is a classifier. Today: how to **judge** it, and what
else is in the toolbox.
:::

## The toolbox, in plain words {.smaller-80}

| Model | How it decides | Can you read it? |
|-----|---------------|-----------|
| **Logistic regression** | one score from a weighted sum of features, turned into a probability | yes: coefficients and odds ratios (week 5). The usual **baseline**: the simple model you start from and try to beat |
| **Decision tree** | a flowchart of simple rules ("age < 30 and visits > 3: likely buyer") | yes: show the tree to a manager |
| **Random forest** | hundreds of trees, each on a random slice of the data; they **vote** | partly: it ranks which features matter, but there are no rules to read |
| **Boosting** (XGBoost) | trees built one after another, each fixing the previous one's mistakes | partly: many settings to get right |
| **Neural network** | layers that learn combinations of features | no: a black box |

::: {.box}
The tradeoff that runs through the whole table: **better predictions vs. a
story you can read**. Forests and boosting usually predict a little better;
the logit is the easiest to explain. Start with the logit, then check
whether the fancy model beats it by enough to matter.
:::

- The leaf's history is the prediction: of the 100 past customers in the

- A **random forest** grows many trees, each on a **random slice** of the
  data, so the trees disagree a little
- For a new customer **every tree votes**, and the forest averages the

:::

## Forests and boosting: one table {.smaller-80}

Both combine many trees. They differ in **how** the trees are built:

| | Random forest | Boosting (XGBoost) |
|---|--------|--------|
| How it works | many trees **in parallel**, each on a random sample; predictions are **averaged** | trees **one after another**; each new tree fixes the previous mistakes |
| What it improves | steadier predictions: one odd tree cannot sway the average | sharper predictions: each tree fixes what the last one missed |
| Tuning | few knobs, works well out of the box | many knobs: how fast it learns, how deep each tree goes, how many trees |
| Risk of memorizing quirks | lower | higher, if not tuned carefully |
| When to use | a fast, strong baseline on noisy data | chasing the best predictions, with time to tune |

# Scoring a Classifier {.divider}

## Every prediction lands in one of four boxes {.smaller-90}

Suppose we predict whether each customer **churns (yes/no)**, and then watch
what actually happens. Four things are possible:

| | Predicted: churn | Predicted: stay |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actually churned** | **true positive (TP)** | **false negative (FN)**, we missed one |
| **Actually stayed** | **false positive (FP)**, false alarm | **true negative (TN)** |

This 2-by-2 count is the **confusion matrix**: every customer falls in
exactly one cell.

::: {.box}
The two mistakes are **not the same mistake**. A false positive wastes a
retention offer on someone who was staying anyway. A false negative lets a
churner walk out the door. Which one costs more depends on the business.
:::

## A worked example: 200 customers {.smaller-90}

Our classifier made a call for 200 customers, and then we watched what
happened:

| | Predicted: churn | Predicted: stay |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actually churned** | 50 (TP) | 10 (FN) |
| **Actually stayed** | 20 (FP) | 120 (TN) |

Three questions, three metrics. Compute them from the table:

- **Accuracy**: what share of all 200 calls were correct?
- **Precision**: of the customers we **called churners**, how many were?
- **Recall**: of the customers who **actually churned**, how many did we catch?

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Take a minute: each answer is one fraction, read straight off the table.
:::

## The same example, computed {.smaller-80}

| | Predicted: churn | Predicted: stay |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actually churned** | 50 (TP) | 10 (FN) |
| **Actually stayed** | 20 (FP) | 120 (TN) |

- **Accuracy** $= \frac{TP + TN}{200} = \frac{50 + 120}{200} = 0.85$:
  the model gets 85% of all calls right
- **Precision** $= \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{50}{50 + 20} = 0.71$:
  when it says "churner", it is right 71% of the time. The other **29% of
  retention offers are wasted** on customers who were staying anyway
- **Recall** $= \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{50}{50 + 10} = 0.83$:
  it catches 83% of the real churners. The other **17% slip away unflagged**

## When accuracy lies {.smaller-80}

Churn is usually **rare**. Say 10,000 customers, **5% churn**: 500 churners,
9,500 stayers. Compare two models:

| Model | Predicted churn | TP | FP | FN | TN | Accuracy | Precision | Recall |
|-----|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| "Nobody churns" | 0 | 0 | 0 | 500 | 9,500 | **95%** | undefined | **0%** |
| A useful model | 600 | 300 | 300 | 200 | 9,200 | **95%** | 50% | 60% |

- The do-nothing model scores **95% accuracy** by predicting "stay" for
  everyone, and catches **zero** churners. Accuracy 95% here means nothing
- The useful model has the **same accuracy**, but it finds 300 of the 500
  churners. Precision and recall see the difference; accuracy cannot

::: {.smaller-90 .muted}
Why "undefined": the first model never says "churn", so there are no churn
calls to grade. Precision would be 0 divided by 0.
:::

::: {.box}
When the "yes" class is rare (churners, clickers, fraud), **never judge a
model by accuracy alone**. Look at precision and recall.
:::

## One number, when you need one: F1 {.smaller-90}

**F1** combines precision and recall into one number between 0 and 1:

$$F1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

- For the useful model above:
  $F1 = 2 \cdot \frac{0.50 \times 0.60}{0.50 + 0.60} = 0.55$
- For the do-nothing model: recall is 0, so **F1 = 0**. The 95% accuracy
  disappears
- F1 is high only when **both** precision and recall are reasonably high:
  few wasted offers **and** few missed churners

::: {.smaller-90 .muted}
Use F1 to rank models with one number when one class is rare. But for
decisions, keep precision and recall separate: they price two different
mistakes.
:::

# Will It Work on New Customers? {.divider}

## The trap: memorizing the past {.smaller-90}

The goal is to predict **new, unseen customers**. The danger is a model that
**memorizes** the old ones instead:

- A flexible model can learn quirks of the data it learned from, like a tree
  that learns "customer #123 always buys". Perfect on the past, **useless**
  for the future
- This is **overfitting**: accuracy on that same old data looks great (even
  100%), and predictions on new customers fail

::: {.box}
A model is only as good as its performance on data it has **never seen**.
Grading it on the data it learned from is letting it grade its own homework.
:::

## The fix: hold some data out {.smaller-90}

**Split the data before fitting** (usually 70/30 or 80/20):

| Set | What it is for |
|---|---------|
| **Training set** | fit the model: estimate coefficients, grow the trees |
| **Test set** | held out, never touched during fitting: it plays the role of **new customers** |

Then compare:

- Accuracy on the training set **much higher** than on the test set:
  **overfitting**
- The two similar: the model **generalizes**, it works beyond the data it
  learned from

::: {.box}
A churn example with real calendar time: train on 2019 to 2024 customers,
test on 2025 customers. If it holds up on 2025, we can trust it for 2026.
:::

## Cross-validation: a fairer check {.smaller-90}

One split can get lucky. **K-fold cross-validation** repeats the check:

1. Split the training data into **k** equal parts, called folds (say k = 5)
2. For each fold: fit the model on the other 4, check the metric (say,
   precision) on the held-out fold
3. **Average** the metric across the 5 folds
4. Pick the model (or tuning) with the best average, then refit on all the
   training data

- Every row gets used for training **and** for validation (in turns)
- Prevents overfitting to **one lucky split**, and compares models fairly

::: {.smaller-90 .muted}
We will not run cross-validation by hand today: R does it in a few lines,
and the exercise sticks to one train/test split. What matters is the idea:
**never grade a model on the data it trained on.**
:::

## Very rare classes: rebalancing the training data {.smaller-80}

Rare classes break accuracy: a few slides ago, the do-nothing model scored
**95%** and caught **zero** churners. Our first fix was better grading:
judge the model by **precision** (how good its "churn" calls are) and
**recall** (how many churners it catches), not by accuracy. When the "yes"
class is **truly scarce** (1% fraud, not 18% churn), there is a second
lever: change what the model **trains on**.

| Option | What it does |
|---|-----------|
| **Oversample** the rare class | repeat the existing churners (or create lookalike ones) in the training set until the model sees them often |
| **Undersample** the common class | drop stayers from the training set |
| **Class weights** | keep the data as it is; tell the model that missing a churner is a bigger mistake than flagging a customer who was going to stay anyway |

- All three push the model to **say "churn" more often**, instead of playing
  it safe with "stay" (the answer that is almost always right when churn is
  rare). So it **catches more real churners (recall up)** and **wastes more
  calls on stayers (precision down)**. Nothing is free; you are choosing
  which mistake to make more often

## Rebalancing: the two rules {.smaller-90}

- Rule 1: rebalance the **training set only**. The test set's job is to
  show how the model will do in the real world, so it must stay as
  imbalanced as reality
- Rule 2: after rebalancing, the **scores come out too high**. Why: a
  model's score for a customer is, roughly, the churn share among the
  **training customers who look like them**, and rebalancing faked that
  share
  - Say 1 of 10 lookalikes churns: the true chance is **10%**. Oversample by
    duplicating that one churner until he appears 9 times: the training data
    now shows 9 churner rows against the 9 stayers, so the model counts
    **9 of 18 = 50%**. The world did not change; the photocopies did that
- The inflation hits everyone, so the **order is still right**: riskier
  customers still score higher. Use the scores to decide **who to call
  first**; just do not read 0.50 as "a 50% chance"

::: {.box}
Rebalancing does not create information that is not in the data. Try the
honest version first: keep the data as it is, grade with precision and
recall, and if the model flags too few churners, lower the bar in the
decision rule (predict churn at a score of 0.2 instead of 0.5).
:::

# A Churn Model, End to End {.divider}

## Our running example: churn at a subscription business {.smaller-80}

**Laptops out: from here we build the model together in R.** Download
[`w9-code.zip`](w9-code.zip) from the course page, open
`w9-1-classifiers-class.R`, and run along; every chart and table on the
slides comes out of that script.

The data: `r format(nrow(churn), big.mark = ",")` customers
of a subscription service, **`r fmt_pct(churn_rate, 1)` churned**. For each
customer we see:

| Feature | Why it should matter |
|------|-----------|
| tenure (months) | long-time customers are safer |
| logins, last 30 days | fewer logins, higher risk |
| support tickets, last 30 days | more tickets, higher risk |
| email engagement (0 to 1) | engaged customers are safer |
| price increase, last 60 days | a price hike raises risk |
| plan downgrade | a downgrade is a warning sign |
| region | small differences across markets |

::: {.box}
Setup: **70/30 split** (`r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` train,
`r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test), then a **logit** on the
training set. Every number that follows is computed on the **test set**:
customers the model has never seen.
:::

## The model's output is a score {.smaller-90}

```{r score-hist}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_hist <- ggplot(test, aes(x = p_logit, fill = factor(churn))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.75, position = "identity", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "grey65", "1" = usc_red),
                    labels = c("stayed", "churned"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Churn Probability on the Test Set",
       x = "Predicted probability of churn (logit)", y = "Customers") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
p_hist
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Each test customer gets a predicted churn probability. Grey: customers who
stayed. Red: customers who actually churned. What do you see?
:::

## Reading the scores {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r score-hist-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.9
p_hist + labs(title = NULL)
```

- The model **separates** the groups, imperfectly: churners (red) pile up at
  higher scores, stayers at lower ones, and the middle **overlaps**
- To act, we must draw a line: a **threshold**. Everyone to the right gets
  the retention offer, everyone to the left does not
- Wherever we draw it, we make both mistakes: some grey to the right
  (wasted offers), some red to the left (missed churners). The threshold
  only chooses the **mix**

## The threshold is a dial {.smaller-90}

```{r sweep-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_sweep <- ggplot(melt(sweep[, .(thr, precision, recall)], id.vars = "thr"),
       aes(x = thr, y = value, color = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(precision = usc_red, recall = blue),
                     labels = c("precision (offers not wasted)",
                                "recall (churners caught)"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Precision and Recall as the Threshold Moves (Logit, Test Set)",
       x = "Threshold: predict churn when score is above...", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
p_sweep
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
The same logit, scored at every threshold from 5% to 60%. What happens to
each line as the threshold rises, and where would you set the dial?
:::

## Reading the dial {.smaller-80 .nostretch}

```{r sweep-chart-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.4
p_sweep + labs(title = NULL)
```

- **Raise the threshold** (only customers with very high scores get called
  churners): the few calls you still make are usually correct, so
  **precision rises**. But real churners with medium scores no longer
  make the cut, so you miss them: **recall falls**
- **Lower the threshold** (customers with even modest scores get called
  churners): you now catch nearly every real churner, so **recall rises**.
  But many of the people you call were going to stay anyway, so
  **precision falls**
- There is no "correct" threshold: it is a **business choice**, and it
  follows from **which mistake costs more**
  - A **wasted offer** costs more (say the offer is a big discount): protect
    **precision**, so raise the threshold
  - A **lost customer** costs more (say each account is worth thousands):
    protect **recall**, so lower it
- 0.5 is just a default: with rare events the useful thresholds sit
  **well below** it

## So how do you pick the threshold? {.smaller-90}

The dial chart is a **menu**, and the business picks from it. Say the
retention team insists that **at least half the offers land on real
churners**:

1. **Turn the goal into a metric target**: the offers go to the customers we
   call churners, so "the share of offers that land on real churners" is,
   word for word, **precision** (of our "churn" calls, how many were right).
   The target: precision at or above 50%, with as much recall as that allows
2. **Read it off the dial chart** (on the test set): the lowest threshold
   that clears 50% precision is **`r fmt_pct(pick$thr)`**
3. **Check what it costs**: at a threshold of `r fmt_pct(pick$thr)`,
   precision is `r fmt_pct(pick$precision, 1)` and recall is
   `r fmt_pct(pick$recall, 1)`: about half the churners still slip through.
   If that is unacceptable, the goal (or the model) has to change

::: {.box}
Different goals pick different spots on the **same chart**: cheap offers
favor recall (set the bar low), expensive offers favor precision (set it
high). And when the team can only make so many calls (say, 90), skip the
threshold entirely: rank the customers by score and work from the top of
the list (coming up in a few slides).
:::

## ROC and AUC: comparing models before choosing a threshold {.smaller-80}

The **ROC curve** traces the whole threshold dial at once: for every
threshold, it plots the share of churners caught (y) against the share of
stayers wrongly called churners (x).

- **Top-left is best**: catch many churners, few false alarms
- The **diagonal** is coin-flipping
- **AUC** (area under the curve) summarizes it in one number: the chance the
  model scores a random churner **above** a random stayer. 0.5 = random,
  1.0 = perfect
- AUC is **threshold-free**: good for comparing models early, before the
  business has picked its threshold

## ROC on our test set: logit vs. random forest {.smaller-90}

```{r roc-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
roc_dt <- rbind(
  data.table(fpr = 1 - roc_logit$specificities, tpr = roc_logit$sensitivities,
             model = sprintf("logit (AUC = %.2f)", auc_logit)),
  data.table(fpr = 1 - roc_rf$specificities, tpr = roc_rf$sensitivities,
             model = sprintf("random forest (AUC = %.2f)", auc_rf)))
p_roc <- ggplot(roc_dt, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, color = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c(usc_red, blue), unique(roc_dt$model)),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "ROC Curves on the Test Set",
       x = "Stayers wrongly flagged (false positive rate)",
       y = "Churners caught (recall)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
p_roc
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Both models, every threshold, one chart. The dashed diagonal is random
guessing. Which model would you take to the retention team?
:::

## Reading the ROC {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r roc-chart-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.9
p_roc + labs(title = NULL)
```

- Both curves sit **well above the diagonal**: either model beats
  coin-flipping by a lot
- The baseline wins: AUC **`r sprintf("%.2f", auc_logit)`** (logit) vs.
  **`r sprintf("%.2f", auc_rf)`** (forest). The churn signal here is mostly
  **simple**: each feature pushes risk up or down on its own, which is
  exactly the kind of pattern a logit captures
- That is a common and useful result: the fancy model is not automatically
  better. When the logit matches or beats the forest, take the logit:
  **the same predictions, plus a story you can read**

## The recipe {.smaller-90}

What we just did, as steps you can rerun on any yes/no problem:

| Step | What to do |
|----|-----------|
| **1. Data** | one row per customer: the outcome (0/1) and the features |
| **2. Split** | 70/30 train/test, before touching any model |
| **3. Fit** | a logit first (the baseline), then a challenger (random forest) |
| **4. Score** | predicted probabilities on the **test set** only |
| **5. Compare** | AUC and the metrics table: does the challenger beat the baseline? |
| **6. Read** | odds ratios (logit), feature importance (forest): what drives risk |
| **7. Act** | pick the threshold that matches the business goal, or rank by score and act on the top of the list |

## Step 5: the metrics table {.smaller-90}

Both models on the test set, threshold at the 0.5 default:

| | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | AUC |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Logit** | `r fmt_pct(m_logit$accuracy, 1)` | `r fmt_pct(m_logit$precision, 1)` | `r fmt_pct(m_logit$recall, 1)` | `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_logit)` |
| **Random forest** | `r fmt_pct(m_rf$accuracy, 1)` | `r fmt_pct(m_rf$precision, 1)` | `r fmt_pct(m_rf$recall, 1)` | `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_rf)` |

- Accuracy looks great for both, but churn is only
  `r fmt_pct(churn_rate, 1)` of customers: we know better than to stop there
- Read the logit row: when it says "churn" it is right
  `r fmt_pct(m_logit$precision, 1)` of the time (precision), but it catches
  only `r fmt_pct(m_logit$recall, 1)` of the real churners (recall). The
  reason: at the 0.5 cutoff it calls just
  **`r m_logit$TP + m_logit$FP` of the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")`**
  test customers churners
- Why so few? Look back at the score histogram: hardly anyone scored above
  50%, so a 0.5 cutoff barely ever fires. The fix is not a new model, it is
  a **lower threshold**: that is exactly how we picked
  `r fmt_pct(pick$thr)` a few slides ago

## Step 6: what drives churn (logit odds ratios) {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r odds-chart}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(or, aes(x = odds, y = label)) +
  geom_col(fill = usc_red, width = 0.65) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", odds)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Odds Ratios from the Logit",
       x = "Odds ratio (dashed line = no effect)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 40%; margin-left: 5%;"}
- Each bar turns a logit coefficient (week 5) into a **multiplier on the
  odds** of churn: a bar at 2.0 means that feature **doubles the odds**,
  holding the others fixed
- Right of the dashed line raises risk: a **plan downgrade** and a recent
  **price increase** are the loudest warnings, and every extra **support
  ticket** adds risk
- Left of the line protects: **engaged** customers and **long-tenure**
  customers churn less
- Week 5 logic, new job: the same odds ratios now tell the retention team
  **what to watch**
:::
:::::

## Step 6: what the forest relied on {.smaller-80}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r importance-chart}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(imp, aes(x = gain, y = label)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = 0.65) +
  labs(title = "Random Forest: Feature Importance",
       x = "Importance (drop in accuracy if the feature is shuffled)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 40%; margin-left: 5%;"}
- The forest has no coefficients to read, so we test a feature by
  **breaking it**: mix up one column at random, so every customer gets
  **someone else's tenure** and the other columns stay put. Same numbers,
  **wrong customers**
- Predict again with the broken column: if the predictions get **much
  worse**, the forest was relying on it. Each bar is that **drop in
  accuracy**; near zero means the feature barely matters
- The ranking broadly **agrees with the logit**: the plan downgrade on top,
  then tenure, logins, and the price increase. Agreement across two
  different models is reassuring
- Importance says **what the model uses**, not why, and not causation:
  shuffling tells us about predictions, not about customers
:::
:::::

## Step 7: act on the scores {.smaller-90}

Suppose the retention team can call **10% of the test customers**
(`r format(K, big.mark = ",")` calls). Skip the threshold: rank by score and
take the **top `r format(K, big.mark = ",")`** (the forest's list):

- **Precision at the top 10%**: `r fmt_pct(prec_k, 1)` of the called
  customers were real churners (vs. a base rate of
  `r fmt_pct(mean(test$churn), 1)` if we called at random)
- **Recall at the top 10%**: the list catches `r fmt_pct(rec_k, 1)` of all
  the churners in the test set
- That is the whole business case in two numbers: **how good the calls
  are**, and **how much of the problem they cover**

::: {.box}
Three ways to run the same model: the default 0.5 cutoff (fine when both
mistakes cost about the same and the outcome is not rare), a threshold
chosen to hit a precision or recall target, or **top-K** when the team can
only handle so many customers. The model gives scores; **the business sets
the dial.**
:::

## What a classifier will not tell you {.smaller-90}

- **Prediction is not causation.** "Support tickets predict churn" does not
  mean tickets cause churn; unhappy customers file tickets *and* leave. The
  model finds **who** is at risk, not **what to change**
- **Garbage in, garbage out.** The model only sees the features you give it;
  a missing driver (a competitor's promo) is invisible
- **The past must look like the future.** A model trained before a price
  change may break after it. Retrain, and re-test, on fresh data
- **A score is not a strategy.** Knowing who will churn is step one; the
  offer, and whether it works, is an experiment (coming later in the course)

## Practice: predicting ad clicks {.smaller-90}

Same recipe, new question: **who clicks the ad?**

- The exercise: fit a logit on
  `r format(nrow(ad), big.mark = ",")` ad impressions, predict clicks at
  the 0.5 cutoff, build the **confusion matrix** by hand, then compute
  **accuracy, precision, recall, and F1**, with questions at every step
- Everything you need, also linked on the course page:
  the **[handout](https://raw.githack.com/dadepro/mkt566/main/w9/case/w9-predicting-ad-click-w-logit.html)**,
  the [R Markdown template](https://github.com/dadepro/mkt566/blob/main/w9/case/w9-predicting-ad-click-w-logit.Rmd),
  and the [data](https://github.com/dadepro/mkt566/blob/main/w9/data/ad_click_data.csv)
  (put the template and the data in **one folder**, then knit)
- One thing to notice: clicks here are
  **`r fmt_pct(mean(ad$click), 1)` of impressions**, not rare. The 0.5
  default behaves reasonably on this data; compare that with our churn data
  (`r fmt_pct(churn_rate, 1)`), where 0.5 barely ever fired
- Work through it before Thursday if you can: it is the best preparation
  for the homework
